az_cochise_stronghold.blurb: Cochise Stronghold fills a rugged stretch of the Dragoon Mountains in southern Arizona with deep canyons, granite domes and spires. Trad leads the way, especially multi-pitch crack lines, with a solid second helping of bouldering and a smaller but real sport scene. Grades run from easy up to the low 5.12s, with the bulk of the roped climbing between 5.9 and 5.11. East Stronghold and West Stronghold split the climbing roughly evenly. This is a big, maze-like backcountry zone where approaches take time and some lines on the larger domes see few ascents, so route-finding matters. Climbing is possible all year; spring and fall are best, winter works on sunny faces, and summer heat limits you to early mornings.

on_ontario_north_bouldering_and_rock.blurb: Northern Ontario climbing is spread across a huge stretch of boreal country, from Sault Ste. Marie and Sudbury in the east to Thunder Bay, Nipigon and Kenora in the northwest, with the Lake Superior shore in between. Sport is the largest share, followed by trad, bouldering and top-rope, plus a real ice scene. Rock varies by place: basalt columns near Nipigon, sandstone at Pass Lake, and granite or gneiss through much of the rest. Rock grades are mostly 5.7 to 5.12, with a heavy cluster around 5.10, and boulder problems mostly in the V0 to V5 range. Many crags are modest and locally developed, so expect variety and plenty of room for exploring.

co_lyons.blurb: Lyons is a small Colorado town whose climbing is mostly up in the St. Vrain Canyons, which follow the South, Middle and North forks of the river. Trad dominates, with a lot of bouldering and a decent amount of sport. The canyons are granite, coarse in places and smoother near Button Rock, while layered sandstone cliffs sit just northwest of town. Most roped routes are fairly short, up to about five pitches, and grades cluster between 5.8 and 5.11, with harder sport lines up to 5.13. Smaller outposts include Camp Dick, Rabbit Mountain and the Lion's Den boulders. Poison ivy and biting flies can be a nuisance in season.

ca_lone_pine_area.blurb: Lone Pine lies on the east side of the Sierra Nevada along US-395, with the High Sierra rising to the west. Most climbing is in the Alabama Hills, a landscape of rounded granite outcrops west of town, where much of the rock is bolted and some of it sits just feet from the car. The mix is sport and trad, with some top-rope and a small amount of bouldering. Grades sit mostly between 5.7 and 5.11, with the busiest stretch around 5.10. Whitney Portal adds longer multi-pitch routes in a cooler setting, while Horseshoe Meadows holds a smaller handful of climbs. The Alabama Hills suit the cooler months, and Whitney Portal is the better pick when it turns hot.

oh_northeast_ohio.blurb: Northeast Ohio is a collection of small ledges, gorges and park outcrops rather than one big cliff. Bouldering is the main event, mostly in the V0 to V5 range, with a good number of top-rope lines and a smaller helping of sport and trad. Roped grades run from easy up to 5.12 and bunch up in the 5.7 to 5.11 band. Chippewa Creek is the biggest bouldering zone, and Whipps Ledges, in Hinckley, is the best-known top-rope venue, with sandstone cliffs of roughly 20 to 50 feet. Sandstone here can turn brittle when wet, so give it a day or two to dry after rain.

ut_maple_canyon.blurb: Maple Canyon in central Utah is best known for steep sport climbing on conglomerate: rounded river cobbles set in a hard matrix, giving holds from jugs to slopers. Nearly everything is bolted, with almost no trad and only a little bouldering. Grades are mostly 5.10 to 5.13, with a fair spread of moderates and a few routes at the top end of the scale. The climbing is spread over the main canyon road and its Left, Middle and Right forks. Winter brings an ice scene too, with mostly WI3 to WI5 lines. Shade from the walls and trees helps on hot days.
